To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
occupational communities and the identity work they engender are important factors in understanding organizational control practices.

the work identities of occupational community members are sustained by a variety of identity work practices and that the control practices used by managers in the organization are not very effective in influencing these identity work practices.

occupational community members, in this case urban police officers, are highly motivated to sustain and sometimes to enhance their work identities, and that they do so in ways that are consistent with the norms of their occupational community and in ways that often frustrate organizational attempts to control the work of these officers.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the interplay of organizational control and occupational identity work in occupational communities.
the interrelationship of work identity, organizational control, and the occupational community.

how the work identities of occupational community members are constructed and reconstructed in their everyday activities, how such work identities are related to the organizational identities and organizational aims, and how the work identities and organizational aims are aligned or misaligned.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

occupational community members do their best to sustain and enhance their valued occupational identities and that managers, in turn, do their best to align the identity-work of occupational community members to organizational aims.
identity work in organizational settings is not only a matter of individual choice but also a matter of organizational control and that the latter is not necessarily as successful as one may wish.
the work identities of occupational community members and their identity work are of central importance for the organizational control of work.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the occupational community is a key site for the production of occupational identities and that these identities in turn are a key resource for the production of organizational identities.
the police officers' occupational identity is a complex, dynamic, and highly contested phenomenon, which is shaped by the officers' interaction with other officers and with members of the community.

occupational communities and occupational identities are not only important for the members of these communities but that they have also been shown to be important to the functioning of the organizations in which these communities are embedded.
The main takeaway from our work is that

occupational community members do not necessarily see themselves as employees of a larger organization, and that the work identities they cultivate and the control strategies that managers employ in their attempts to align these identities with the goals of the organization are not necessarily compatible.
organizational control practices are not necessarily effective in the management of occupational communities.
the identities of occupational community members are not easily controlled by organizational authorities.
